slides.title: Asking kindly
slides.text: When you want something, ask with words instead of grabbing. For example: "Can I have a turn when you're done?"

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to play with a toy someone else has. What's a good way to ask?

options.label: Ask with kind words instead of grabbing
options.outcome: Exactly right! When you want something, asking with words instead of grabbing is the kind, fair way to do it.

options.label: Just grab the toy
options.outcome: Grabbing isn't fair to the other person — asking with kind words is the better approach.

options.label: Wait and never ask at all
options.outcome: Never asking means you'll never get a turn — asking kindly is the way to go.

slides.title: Listen to the answer
slides.text: After you ask, listen to the answer. Your friend might say "yes," "not yet," or "no," and you can decide what to do next.

widgetConfig.scenario: You ask a friend for a turn with the toy, and they say 'not yet.' What should you do next?

options.label: Listen to their answer and wait a bit
options.outcome: Exactly right! After you ask, listening to the answer — even if it's 'not yet' — is the kind and fair thing to do.

options.label: Ignore what they said and take it anyway
options.outcome: Ignoring their answer and taking it isn't fair — listening and waiting is the better choice.

options.label: Get upset and stop being friends
options.outcome: Getting upset over a simple 'not yet' isn't necessary — listening and waiting a bit works much better.

slides.title: Taking turns
slides.text: When two people want the same toy, taking turns can help. You might play with the truck first, then give your friend a turn.

widgetConfig.scenario: You and a friend both want the same toy truck. What can help?

options.label: Take turns playing with it
options.outcome: Exactly right! When two people want the same toy, taking turns can help both of you enjoy it.

options.label: Grab it and refuse to share
options.outcome: Grabbing and refusing to share isn't fair — taking turns works much better for both of you.

options.label: Taking turns never helps
options.outcome: Taking turns actually helps a lot — it's a simple, fair way for both friends to get a turn.

slides.title: Please and thank you
slides.text: Kind words make asking feel friendly. You can say "please" when you ask and "thank you" when someone shares or listens.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want a grown-up to get you a snack. What's the best way to ask?

options.label: "Can I please have a snack?"
options.outcome: Perfect! Saying please makes your request polite and more likely to get a yes.

options.label: "Give me a snack now!"
options.outcome: Demanding without please can come across as rude — asking politely usually works better.

options.label: Just grab a snack without asking
options.outcome: Asking first, with please, is more polite than just taking something.

slides.title: Know what you want
slides.text: Before you ask, think about what you want. Do you want the blue crayon, a turn on the swing, or help opening something?

widgetConfig.prompt: Which of these is NOT a good first step before asking for something?

items.label: Think about what you really want
Think about what the other person might want too
Decide what you'd be happy with

widgetConfig.explanation: Grabbing without thinking skips the whole point of negotiating — thinking first about what you and the other person want leads to a much better outcome.

slides.title: Sharing the tablet
slides.text: If you and your sibling both want the tablet, make a turn plan. For example: ten minutes for you, then ten minutes for them.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're playing on the tablet and your sibling wants a turn too. What's a good way to handle it?

options.label: Agree on a time, like "5 more minutes, then your turn"
options.outcome: That's a great plan — agreeing on a fair time means you both get a turn without a fight.

options.label: Say "No, it's mine!" and keep playing
options.outcome: Holding on without talking it through usually leads to an argument. Agreeing on a turn works better for both of you.

options.label: Give it up right away even though you wanted more time
options.outcome: You don't have to give up what you want completely — finding a fair middle ground works for everyone.

slides.title: Waiting for your turn
slides.text: Sometimes you have to wait. You can ask, "Can I go after you?" and do something else until it is your turn.

widgetConfig.scenario: You have to wait for your turn on the swing. What can you do while waiting?

options.label: Ask "Can I go after you?" and do something else meanwhile
options.outcome: Exactly right! You can ask when your turn will be and do something else while you wait.

options.label: Push past and take it anyway
options.outcome: Pushing past isn't fair to the person already swinging — asking and waiting is the better choice.

options.label: Waiting is never necessary
options.outcome: Waiting your turn is actually an important part of sharing — sometimes you do have to wait.

slides.title: Use your words
slides.text: If someone has something that belongs to you, ask for it back calmly. Try: "Can I have my toy back, please?"

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone has your toy. What's a calm way to ask for it back?

options.label: Say "Can I have my toy back, please?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Asking calmly for something that belongs to you works well.

options.label: Grab it without asking
options.outcome: Grabbing it without asking isn't calm — using your words to ask works much better.

options.label: Yell to get it back
options.outcome: Yelling isn't necessary — asking calmly with your words works just as well, and more kindly.

slides.title: Ask a grown-up for help
slides.text: If you cannot solve a problem safely or fairly, ask a trusted grown-up for help. Getting help is part of solving the problem.

widgetConfig.scenario: You can't solve a problem safely or fairly on your own. What should you do?

options.label: Ask a trusted grown-up for help
options.outcome: Exactly right! If you cannot solve a problem safely or fairly, asking a trusted grown-up for help is part of solving it.

options.label: Never ask anyone for help
options.outcome: Never asking for help can leave a problem unsolved — asking a trusted grown-up is a smart move.

options.label: Getting help means you failed
options.outcome: Getting help doesn't mean you failed — it's a normal, smart part of solving tricky problems.

quiz.question: What is the first step to getting a yes when you want something?
choices: Asking nicely
Grabbing it
quiz.explanation: Asking kindly is the best first step because it tells the other person what you want without grabbing. They may say yes, not yet, or no.

quiz.question: You ask for the ball and your friend says "in two minutes." What should you do?
choices: Listen to what the other person says
Cover your ears
quiz.explanation: Listening helps you understand why. Maybe your friend just needs two more minutes with the ball.

quiz.question: You and a friend both want the same red truck. What can you do?
choices: Take turns
Fight over it
quiz.explanation: Taking turns means everyone gets to play. You go first, then your friend gets the truck.

quiz.question: Before you ask for something, what should you do first?
choices: Think about what you really want
Just grab it right away
quiz.explanation: Thinking first helps you ask for the right thing, like the blue cup instead of any cup.

quiz.question: You ask your friend for a turn. What should you say?
choices: Please, and thank you after
Nothing, just take it
quiz.explanation: Saying please and thank you keeps things kind, even when the answer is no.

quiz.question: You and your sibling both want the tablet. What is fair?
choices: Take turns, ten minutes each
Whoever grabs it first keeps it
quiz.explanation: Taking turns gives both people a chance to use the tablet. A simple timer can help you remember when to switch.

quiz.question: You are waiting for a turn on the swing. What should you do?
choices: Ask to go next and wait safely
Push the other child off
quiz.explanation: Ask to go next, then wait safely until the swing is free. Waiting does not mean you can decide when someone else's turn must end.

quiz.question: Your friend has a toy you want. What should you do?
choices: Use your words and ask
Grab it out of their hands
quiz.explanation: Using your words works better than grabbing. Asking nicely feels kinder to your friend.

quiz.question: You and a friend cannot agree on a game. What can help?
choices: Ask a grown-up to help you decide
Stop being friends
quiz.explanation: A grown-up can help you find a fair answer, like playing one game, then the other.

quiz.question: Your sibling is explaining why they are upset. What should you do?
choices: Listen carefully
Interrupt and walk away
quiz.explanation: Listening carefully helps you understand how someone feels, like why your sibling is upset.

slides.title: Make a fair trade
slides.text: A trade should feel okay to both people. If you swap crayons, both of you should want the crayon you are getting.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want your sibling's toy car, and they want your extra sticker. What makes this trade fair?

options.label: Both of you agree and feel happy with the swap
options.outcome: Exactly right! A fair trade means both people agree and feel good about what they're getting.

options.label: Only you get something you want
options.outcome: A fair trade means both sides get something they're happy with, not just one person.

options.label: Taking it without asking
options.outcome: That's not trading at all — a real trade means both people agree to swap.

slides.title: Try another idea
slides.text: If your first idea does not work, try a different one. If your friend does not want to trade toys, maybe you can play with them together.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your friend doesn't want to trade toys. What can you try instead?

options.label: Suggest playing with the toys together
options.outcome: Exactly right! If your first idea doesn't work, trying a different one, like playing together, can work out well.

options.label: Give up on playing together entirely
options.outcome: Giving up entirely skips a chance to find a different idea that works for both of you.

options.label: Insist on the same idea over and over
options.outcome: Insisting on the same idea that already didn't work rarely helps — trying something different works better.

slides.title: Meet in the middle
slides.text: A compromise means both people change their plan a little. You could play tag first and hide-and-seek next.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to play tag, your friend wants hide-and-seek. What's a compromise?

options.label: Play tag first, then hide-and-seek
options.outcome: Exactly right! A compromise means both people change their plan a little, like playing both games.

options.label: Only ever play your own choice
options.outcome: Only playing your own choice isn't a compromise — changing your plan a little helps both of you.

options.label: Compromise means one person never gets their way
options.outcome: A real compromise means both people get something, not that one person never gets their way.

slides.title: It is okay to hear no
slides.text: Sometimes the answer is no. You can feel disappointed and still stay calm, kind, and safe.

widgetConfig.scenario: You ask a friend to trade toys, but they say no. How should you feel about that?

options.label: It's okay — they're allowed to say no, and that's okay
options.outcome: Exactly right! Everyone can say no to a trade, and that's a normal part of asking.

options.label: Get upset and demand they trade anyway
options.outcome: A no means no — getting upset about it isn't fair to your friend's choice.

options.label: Never ask anyone to trade again
options.outcome: One no doesn't mean you should stop asking others — it's just a normal part of trading sometimes.

slides.title: Split a big job
slides.text: A big job can be shared. One person can pick up the toys while the other puts the books away.

widgetConfig.scenario: There's a big cleanup job: toys and books. How can two people share it?

options.label: One picks up toys while the other puts away books
options.outcome: Exactly right! A big job can be shared, with each person taking part of the work.

options.label: One person does everything alone
options.outcome: Doing everything alone makes a big job much harder — sharing it between two people works better.

options.label: Sharing a job never helps
options.outcome: Sharing a job actually helps a lot — it makes a big cleanup much easier for everyone.

slides.title: You can say no to a trade
slides.text: You never have to make a trade that feels wrong or unfair. You can say, "No thanks, I want to keep mine."

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone wants to trade toys, but it feels unfair to you. What can you do?

options.label: Say "No thanks, I want to keep mine"
options.outcome: Exactly right! You never have to make a trade that feels wrong or unfair.

options.label: Trade even though it feels wrong
options.outcome: Trading something that feels unfair isn't necessary — you can say no if it doesn't feel right.

options.label: You must always agree to a trade
options.outcome: You don't have to always agree — saying no to a trade that feels unfair is perfectly okay.

slides.title: Only trade if both agree
slides.text: A fair trade needs two yeses. If either person changes their mind before the trade happens, the trade should stop.

widgetConfig.scenario: You and a friend are trading toys, but your friend suddenly says they changed their mind before you swap. What should happen?

options.label: The trade shouldn't happen since both people need to agree
options.outcome: Exactly right! A fair trade needs both people to say yes — if someone changes their mind, the trade shouldn't go through.

options.label: The trade should happen anyway since you already agreed
options.outcome: A trade needs both people to still agree right up until it happens — if someone changes their mind, it shouldn't go through.

options.label: Whoever decides first should win
options.outcome: Trades aren't about who decides first — both people need to agree for it to be fair.

slides.title: Choose together
slides.text: If you want different games, make a plan that includes both people. Play one game first and the other one next.

widgetConfig.scenario: You and a friend want to play different games. What's a fair plan?

options.label: Play one game first, then the other
options.outcome: Exactly right! Making a plan that includes both games means both people get to play what they want.

options.label: Only ever play your own game
options.outcome: Only playing your own choice leaves your friend out — making a plan that includes both is fairer.

options.label: Choosing together never works
options.outcome: Choosing together actually works well — it lets both people get a turn with their favorite game.

slides.title: Feelings are okay
slides.text: You will not always get your first choice. It is okay to feel sad or frustrated while still speaking kindly.

widgetConfig.scenario: You didn't get your first choice. Is it okay to feel sad about it?

options.label: Yes — you can feel sad while still speaking kindly
options.outcome: Exactly right! You will not always get your first choice, and it's okay to feel sad or frustrated while still being kind.

options.label: No, you must pretend to feel fine
options.outcome: You don't have to pretend — it's okay to feel sad, as long as you still speak kindly.

options.label: Feeling sad means you should be unkind
options.outcome: Feeling sad doesn't mean you should be unkind — you can feel your feelings while still speaking kindly.

quiz.question: You trade your red crayon for a friend's blue one. What should a trade feel like?
choices: Fair to both people
Only good for one person
quiz.explanation: A fair trade needs both people to choose it. If either person does not want the trade, it should not happen.

quiz.question: Your friend says no to your game idea. What can you do?
choices: Try a new idea instead
Give up and go home
quiz.explanation: Trying a new idea can help you find something fun together, like playing tag instead.

quiz.question: You want tag, your friend wants hide and seek, so you agree to play both. What is this called?
choices: A compromise — both people give a little
Only one person gets what they want
quiz.explanation: In a compromise, both people give a little. Playing tag first, then hide and seek, makes you both happy.

quiz.question: Your friend says no. What should you do?
choices: Stay calm and try again later
Yell and grab it
quiz.explanation: Staying calm keeps things friendly, even after a no. You can always ask again later.

quiz.question: You and your sibling share a big chore. What helps make it fair?
choices: Split the job into two parts
Make one person do it all
quiz.explanation: Splitting the job means it isn't too hard for one person, like sharing toy pickup and table wiping.

quiz.question: A trade feels bad to you. What can you do?
choices: Say no and walk away
Trade anyway even though it feels bad
quiz.explanation: You can say no to a trade that does not feel right to you. You do not have to trade just to be polite.

quiz.question: What does a fair trade need?
choices: Both people freely agree
One person keeps asking until the other says yes
quiz.explanation: A fair trade needs two real yeses. Pressure does not make a trade fair.

quiz.question: You want to play blocks, your sibling wants a puzzle. What can you do?
choices: Take turns picking which to play first
Only ever play blocks
quiz.explanation: Taking turns picking means you both get to enjoy your favorite game, like blocks today and puzzles tomorrow.

quiz.question: You don't get to pick the game today. How should you feel and act?
choices: It's okay to feel sad, but stay calm and kind
Yell and cry until you get your way
quiz.explanation: It's okay to feel sad when you don't get your way, but staying calm and kind still matters.

quiz.question: What happens when both people compromise?
choices: Both people get some of what they want
One person gets everything
quiz.explanation: When both people compromise, everyone gives a little and everyone gets something, like sharing turns on a toy.

slides.title: What is negotiation?
slides.text: Negotiation is a conversation where people try to find a plan they can both accept. If you want a movie and your sibling wants a game, you might agree on game first and movie after.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want a movie, your sibling wants a game. What does negotiation look like here?

options.label: Finding a plan you can both accept, like game first then movie
options.outcome: Exactly right! Negotiation is a conversation where people try to find a plan they can both accept.

options.label: Whoever asks first always wins
options.outcome: Negotiation isn't about who asks first — it's about finding a plan both people can accept.

options.label: Negotiation means one person always gives up everything
options.outcome: Negotiation isn't about one person giving up everything — it's about finding something that works for both.

slides.title: Listen for the reason
slides.text: Do not only listen to what someone wants—listen for why. If your sibling needs the game at 6:00 because a friend is joining online, you can plan your movie for before or after that time.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your sibling wants the video game controller right now. Instead of just saying no, what's a better first step?

options.label: Ask why they need it right now
options.outcome: Exactly! Listening for the reason behind a request helps you find a solution that actually works for both of you.

options.label: Say no immediately without asking anything
options.outcome: Saying no right away misses the chance to understand their reason, which could help you find a solution together.

options.label: Give in immediately without asking why
options.outcome: Giving in without understanding the reason means you might miss a better solution for both of you.

slides.title: Explain your reason
slides.text: A reason helps the other person understand your request. "Can I have 20 more minutes because I am almost finished with this level?" is clearer than "I just want more time."

widgetConfig.scenario: You want 20 more minutes of screen time. Which request works better?

options.label: "Can I have 20 more minutes because I'm almost finished with this level?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A reason helps the other person understand your request and makes it clearer.

options.label: "I just want more time"
options.outcome: A request with no reason is less clear — explaining why makes it much easier to understand.

options.label: Reasons never help a request
options.outcome: Reasons actually help a lot — they make your request clearer and easier for someone to consider.

slides.title: Know your goal
slides.text: Before you ask, decide what you really need. Maybe you do not need a later bedtime every night—you only want to finish one special movie tonight.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to negotiate more time before bedtime. What should you figure out first?

options.label: What you actually want — like 15 more minutes to read
options.outcome: Exactly! Knowing your specific goal helps you make a clear, reasonable ask instead of just complaining.

options.label: Just complain about bedtime being unfair
options.outcome: Complaining without a clear goal rarely leads anywhere — knowing exactly what you want to ask for works better.

options.label: Demand to stay up as late as you want
options.outcome: An unreasonable demand is less likely to work — a clear, specific, reasonable goal (like 15 more minutes) is more effective.

slides.title: Think of more than one option
slides.text: One idea may not work, so bring two or three possibilities. You might suggest watching half the movie now, finishing it tomorrow, or choosing a shorter movie.

widgetConfig.prompt: Which of these is NOT an example of having more than one option?

items.label: Suggesting trading toys instead of just asking for one
Only ever asking the exact same way every time
Proposing a different time that works for both

widgetConfig.explanation: Only ever asking the same way doesn't give you more options — the other three show flexible ways to think of alternatives.

slides.title: Ask useful questions
slides.text: If someone says no, do not immediately argue. Ask, "What part does not work for you?" or "What would make this feel fair?"

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone says no to your idea. What's a better response than arguing?

options.label: Ask "What part doesn't work for you?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Instead of immediately arguing, asking what doesn't work helps you understand and find a better plan.

options.label: Argue back immediately
options.outcome: Arguing back right away skips a chance to understand their concern — asking a useful question works better.

options.label: Just accept it and never ask why
options.outcome: Accepting a no without ever asking why means missing a chance to find a plan that could work for both of you.

slides.title: Stay calm when you disagree
slides.text: A calm brain solves problems better. If voices get louder, pause, breathe, and come back to the problem instead of attacking the person.

widgetConfig.scenario: You and a friend disagree about which game to play at recess. You're starting to feel frustrated. What should you do?

options.label: Take a breath and calmly explain why you want your game
options.outcome: Staying calm helps you actually get heard — when you're calm, it's much easier to find an option you both like.

options.label: Raise your voice to make your point
options.outcome: Getting loud can make the other person defensive instead of open to compromise.

options.label: Storm off without saying anything
options.outcome: Walking away without explaining leaves the disagreement unsolved — a calm conversation works better.

slides.title: Make a screen-time plan
slides.text: Rules made before an argument starts are easier to follow. You and a sibling might agree on 30-minute turns and decide who goes first.

widgetConfig.scenario: You and a sibling keep arguing about screen time. What helps?

options.label: Agree on rules, like 30-minute turns, before an argument starts
options.outcome: Exactly right! Rules made before an argument starts are easier to follow than rules made in the heat of the moment.

options.label: Make rules only in the middle of an argument
options.outcome: Making rules in the middle of an argument is much harder — agreeing on a plan ahead of time works better.

options.label: Rules never help with sharing screen time
options.outcome: Rules actually help a lot with sharing screen time, especially when agreed on calmly ahead of time.

slides.title: A no can give you information
slides.text: A no does not always mean "never." Ask politely why, listen to the reason, and see whether a different plan could work.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone says no to your plan. Does 'no' always mean 'never'?

options.label: No — politely asking why can reveal a different plan that could work
options.outcome: Exactly right! A no doesn't always mean never — asking politely why and listening can reveal a plan that works.

options.label: Yes, no always means never
options.outcome: A no doesn't always mean never — it can be worth asking why and seeing if a different plan would work.

options.label: Asking why after a no is pointless
options.outcome: Asking why after a no can actually be very useful — it might reveal a plan that works for everyone.

quiz.question: You want a movie, your sibling wants a game. What is negotiation?
choices: Talking to find an answer that works for both people
Insisting on getting your own way
quiz.explanation: Negotiation means talking until you find a plan that works for both people. If you want a movie and your sibling wants a game, you might watch first and play after.

quiz.question: You learn your sibling wants the game because a friend is joining online at a specific time. Why is that helpful to know?
choices: It helps you understand what they want and why
It wastes time
quiz.explanation: Knowing the reason helps you plan around what matters. If the game must happen at a set time, your movie can happen before or after it.

quiz.question: Instead of only suggesting one idea for tonight's TV time, you also suggest two backups. Why brainstorm more than one option?
choices: It's more likely you'll find one that works for everyone
One idea is always enough
quiz.explanation: Thinking of several ideas instead of just one raises your odds of finding something that works. Offering both "half the movie now" and "game after" gives your sibling more choices.

quiz.question: A negotiation over TV time starts to get heated. What helps most?
choices: Staying calm and taking a breath
Getting upset right away
quiz.explanation: Staying calm helps you think clearly instead of just reacting. Taking a breath before you speak makes it easier to actually solve the problem.

quiz.question: Before asking for something, what should you figure out first?
choices: What you actually want and why
Nothing, just ask right away
quiz.explanation: Knowing what you want and why makes your request clearer and stronger. Saying "I want a later bedtime because of movie night" works better than just asking.

quiz.question: Screen time causes arguments between you and your sibling. What can help?
choices: Agreeing on a schedule ahead of time
Whoever asks first always wins
quiz.explanation: Agreeing on a schedule ahead of time stops arguments before they even start. If you and your sibling both know it's thirty minutes each, there's nothing left to fight about.

quiz.question: Your idea gets turned down. What works better than arguing?
choices: Staying calm and asking a follow-up question
Arguing louder until they give in
quiz.explanation: Asking a calm question keeps the conversation open instead of turning it into a fight. Asking "what would make this work for you?" often turns a no into a new idea.

quiz.question: You want thirty more minutes of game time. What makes your ask stronger?
choices: Explaining why you want it
Just repeating "please" over and over
quiz.explanation: Explaining your reason makes it easier for someone to say yes. "I want thirty more minutes because I'm almost done" works better than just asking for more time.

quiz.question: Your sibling says no to your plan. What is a good next step?
choices: Ask what would make it work for them
Walk away angry and stop talking
quiz.explanation: A calm follow-up question can help you understand why the plan does not work. Sometimes that leads to a different idea; sometimes the answer is still no.

quiz.question: Why come up with two or three ideas instead of just one?
choices: It raises your odds of finding something that works
It just wastes everyone's time
quiz.explanation: Having backup ideas ready raises your odds of landing on a plan everyone likes. If your first idea gets turned down, you already have another one ready to offer.

slides.title: What makes a trade fair?
slides.text: A fair trade is one both people choose freely and understand. Nobody should feel tricked, rushed, or pressured into saying yes.

widgetConfig.scenario: You and a friend want to swap toys. What makes this trade fair?

options.label: Both people choose freely and understand what they are trading
options.outcome: Exactly! A fair trade is one both people choose freely and understand — nobody should feel tricked or pressured.

options.label: Whoever insists the loudest wins the trade
options.outcome: Fairness isn't about who insists loudest — both people choosing freely and understanding the trade is what matters.

options.label: Fairness does not matter in trades
options.outcome: Fairness actually matters a lot — a trade both people freely agree to and understand is what makes it fair.

slides.title: Check before trading
slides.text: Before you swap toys, cards, or snacks, make sure both people know exactly what is being traded and both still want to do it.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend offers to trade you a toy, but you haven't looked closely at it yet. What should you do before agreeing?

options.label: Check it out closely first to make sure it's what you want
options.outcome: Smart move! Checking before trading helps make sure you're happy with the deal.

options.label: Agree right away without looking
options.outcome: Agreeing without checking first could mean a surprise you don't like — looking first is smarter.

options.label: Never trade anything ever
options.outcome: You can still trade! Just check things out first so you know what you're getting.

slides.title: Meet in the middle
slides.text: Sometimes two offers can meet halfway. If you ask for 30 extra minutes and your guardian offers 10, you might agree on 20.

widgetConfig.scenario: You ask for 30 extra minutes and your guardian offers 10. What's a middle option?

options.label: Agree on 20 minutes
options.outcome: Exactly right! Sometimes two offers can meet halfway, like agreeing on 20 minutes between 30 and 10.

options.label: Insist on the full 30 or nothing
options.outcome: Insisting on all-or-nothing skips a chance to find a middle ground that works for both of you.

options.label: Meeting in the middle never works
options.outcome: Meeting in the middle actually works well — it's a simple way to find an agreement both sides can accept.

slides.title: Look for a win-win
slides.text: A win-win does not mean everyone gets everything. It means both people get something important enough to feel okay with the result.

widgetConfig.scenario: Does a win-win mean everyone gets everything they wanted?

options.label: No — it means both people get something important enough to feel okay
options.outcome: Exactly right! A win-win doesn't mean everyone gets everything — it means both sides get something that matters enough to them.

options.label: Yes, everyone always gets everything
options.outcome: A win-win doesn't mean getting everything — it means both people get something meaningful enough to feel okay.

options.label: A win-win is impossible
options.outcome: A win-win is actually possible in many situations — it just means both sides get something that matters.

slides.title: Split chores by effort
slides.text: Fair does not always mean identical. One person might vacuum while the other empties trash and wipes the table, then you can switch next time.

widgetConfig.scenario: Does splitting chores fairly always mean doing identical tasks?

options.label: No — one vacuums while the other empties trash, and you switch later
options.outcome: Exactly right! Fair does not always mean identical — different tasks can be split fairly and switched later.

options.label: Yes, fair always means exactly identical tasks
options.outcome: Fair doesn't always mean identical — different tasks of similar effort can be split fairly too.

options.label: Splitting chores by effort never works
options.outcome: Splitting chores by effort actually works well — it lets each person take on a fair share, even if the tasks differ.

slides.title: Make room for every voice
slides.text: In a group, the loudest person should not automatically decide. Let everyone explain what matters to them before choosing a plan.

widgetConfig.scenario: In a group decision, should the loudest person automatically decide?

options.label: No — let everyone explain what matters to them first
options.outcome: Exactly right! In a group, the loudest person should not automatically decide — everyone should get to explain what matters to them.

options.label: Yes, the loudest voice should always win
options.outcome: The loudest voice shouldn't automatically win — letting everyone explain what matters leads to better group decisions.

options.label: Only one person's opinion ever matters
options.outcome: Everyone's opinion matters in a group decision, not just one person's.

slides.title: Pause when you cannot agree
slides.text: If a conversation is going nowhere, it is okay to stop and try again later. A break can help everyone think more clearly.

widgetConfig.scenario: A conversation is going nowhere and getting frustrating. What can help?

options.label: Stop and try again later
options.outcome: Exactly right! If a conversation is going nowhere, it's okay to stop and try again later — a break can help everyone think more clearly.

options.label: Keep pushing until someone gives in
options.outcome: Pushing until someone gives in can make things worse — pausing and returning later often works much better.

options.label: Pausing never helps a disagreement
options.outcome: Pausing actually helps a lot — a break can give everyone time to think more clearly before trying again.

slides.title: You are allowed to say no
slides.text: Negotiation does not mean you must agree. If a plan does not work for you, you can say no calmly and explain your reason if you want to.

widgetConfig.scenario: Does negotiating mean you must always agree to the plan?

options.label: No — you can say no calmly and explain your reason
options.outcome: Exactly right! Negotiation does not mean you must agree — if a plan doesn't work for you, you can say no calmly.

options.label: Yes, you must always agree
options.outcome: You don't have to always agree — if a plan doesn't work for you, saying no calmly is completely fine.

options.label: Saying no is never allowed in a negotiation
options.outcome: Saying no is actually allowed and sometimes necessary — negotiation doesn't require always agreeing.

slides.title: Walk away from pressure
slides.text: If someone keeps pushing after you say no, ending the conversation is okay. A fair deal does not require pressure.

widgetConfig.scenario: A friend keeps pushing you to trade your favorite toy for something you don't really want. What should you do?

options.label: Politely say no and walk away if they keep pushing
options.outcome: Great choice! You never have to agree to a trade just because someone keeps asking — walking away is okay.

options.label: Give in just to make them stop asking
options.outcome: You don't have to give in to pressure — it's okay to keep saying no, even if someone keeps asking.

options.label: Get angry and yell at them
options.outcome: A calm 'no' and walking away works better than getting angry — you're allowed to just decline.

quiz.question: You do your sibling's dishes in exchange for picking the movie tonight. What makes this a fair trade?
choices: Both people feel like they gained something
Only one person benefits
quiz.explanation: A fair trade leaves both people feeling like they gained something good. You do the dishes, and in return you get to pick the movie tonight.

quiz.question: You ask for 30 extra minutes, your guardian offers 10, and you agree on 20. What does "splitting the difference" mean?
choices: Meeting in the middle between two offers
One side getting everything
quiz.explanation: Splitting the difference means landing between two starting offers. If you ask for thirty minutes and get offered ten, meeting at twenty feels fair to both sides.

quiz.question: What is a "win-win" outcome?
choices: Both sides end up happy
One side gets everything and the other gets nothing
quiz.explanation: Splitting the difference means choosing a point between two offers. It can be useful, although the middle is not automatically fair in every situation.

quiz.question: Two people share a big chore. What helps keep it fair?
choices: Splitting the job and switching tasks later
Only one person doing all of it
quiz.explanation: Splitting the job and switching tasks later keeps things fair over time. Vacuuming this week and emptying trash next week means neither person is stuck with the harder job forever.

quiz.question: A trade does not feel fair to you. What can you do?
choices: Say no and walk away
Agree anyway so you do not seem rude
quiz.explanation: It's okay to walk away from a deal that doesn't feel fair to you. Saying no calmly is better than agreeing and feeling bad about it later.

quiz.question: You trade your board game for a friend's video game, but only because you feel pressured. Is that a fair trade?
choices: No, because you don't feel excited about it
Yes, any trade that happens is fair
quiz.explanation: A fair trade should be freely chosen by both people. If you feel pressured, you can stop and say no.

quiz.question: You and a sibling truly cannot agree tonight. What can you do?
choices: Stop and agree to talk again later
Keep arguing until someone gives in
quiz.explanation: Stopping and coming back later is often better than pushing through an argument. Saying "let's each do something else tonight and talk tomorrow" gives everyone time to cool off.

quiz.question: A trade doesn't work for you. What can you say?
choices: No, calmly and completely
Nothing, you have to accept it
quiz.explanation: You are allowed to say no to a deal that does not work for you. You do not owe anyone an agreement just because they asked.

quiz.question: You're negotiating TV time with two siblings at once. What should you look for?
choices: A plan that works for everyone at the table
Whatever the loudest person wants
quiz.explanation: A good group plan works for everyone at the table, not just whoever talks the loudest. Taking turns choosing shows helps every sibling feel included.

quiz.question: Why switch chore tasks with your sibling from week to week?
choices: It keeps things fair over time
It doesn't matter who does what
quiz.explanation: Switching tasks over time keeps the arrangement fair to both people. Nobody gets stuck doing the harder chore, like taking out trash, every single week.

slides.title: Positions vs. interests
slides.text: A position is what someone says they want; an interest is the reason underneath it. "I want the tablet now" is a position. "I need to finish homework before practice" is the interest—and that reason may lead to a better solution.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your sibling insists on "I want the window seat" (their position), but what they actually care about is getting fresh air (their interest). How should you use this?

options.label: Address the real interest — maybe cracking a window works for everyone
options.outcome: Exactly — understanding the interest behind a position often reveals solutions neither side considered, like a different way to get fresh air.

options.label: Just argue about who gets the window seat
options.outcome: Focusing only on the stated position (the seat) misses the real interest (fresh air) — which might have an easier solution.

options.label: Ignore what they actually want
options.outcome: Understanding the real interest behind their request often leads to a solution that satisfies everyone, not just a win/lose fight over the position.

slides.title: Prepare before you ask
slides.text: Think through your goal, your reason, and what the other person may care about. Before asking for a later curfew, for example, consider transportation, safety, and how you will check in.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to ask for something important. What helps before the conversation even starts?

options.label: Thinking through your goal, your reason, and what the other person may care about
options.outcome: Exactly right! Thinking through your goal, your reason, and what the other person may care about helps you prepare well.

options.label: Walking in with no thought beforehand
options.outcome: Walking in with no preparation makes the conversation harder — thinking it through first helps a lot.

options.label: Preparation never actually helps a negotiation
options.outcome: Preparation actually helps a great deal — thinking through your goal and reasons beforehand sets you up for success.

slides.title: Use active listening
slides.text: Active listening means checking that you understood correctly. Saying, "So your main concern is how I will get home safely—is that right?" can prevent you from arguing about the wrong problem.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to check you understood someone's concern correctly. What helps?

options.label: Say "So your main concern is X — is that right?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Active listening means checking that you understood correctly, which can prevent arguing about the wrong problem.

options.label: Assume you already know what they meant
options.outcome: Assuming you already know can lead to arguing about the wrong problem — checking your understanding works better.

options.label: Active listening never prevents misunderstandings
options.outcome: Active listening actually helps prevent misunderstandings — checking you understood correctly clears things up.

slides.title: Know your real goal
slides.text: Sometimes your first request is bigger than what you actually need. If you only need one late night for a concert, asking for that may work better than asking to change your curfew permanently.

widgetConfig.scenario: You only need one late night for a concert, but you're about to ask to change your curfew permanently. What's smarter?

options.label: Ask for just the one late night you actually need
options.outcome: Exactly right! Sometimes your first request is bigger than what you actually need — asking for exactly what you need may work better.

options.label: Always ask for the biggest possible change
options.outcome: Asking for more than you actually need can make the request harder to get — asking for what you really need often works better.

options.label: Your real goal never matters in a negotiation
options.outcome: Your real goal actually matters a lot — knowing it helps you ask for exactly what you need.

slides.title: Ask open-ended questions
slides.text: Questions like "What would make this work for you?" reveal more than yes-or-no questions. They help you discover concerns you may not have noticed.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want to understand why your friend won't agree to your plan. Which question works better?

options.label: "What's making you hesitant about this plan?"
options.outcome: Great choice — an open-ended question invites them to explain their real concerns, which helps you find a solution.

options.label: "Do you like my plan or not?"
options.outcome: That's a yes/no question that doesn't reveal their actual concerns — an open question uncovers more useful information.

options.label: Don't ask anything, just assume you know why
options.outcome: Assuming instead of asking can lead to misunderstanding their real concern — asking helps you actually understand.

slides.title: Separate wants from needs
slides.text: A need is something important for the situation to work; a want is a preference. You may need a reliable laptop for school but only want the newest model.

widgetConfig.scenario: You need a reliable laptop for school but just want the newest model. What's the difference?

options.label: A need is important for things to work; a want is a preference
options.outcome: Exactly right! A need is something important for the situation to work, while a want is a preference.

options.label: Needs and wants are exactly the same thing
options.outcome: Needs and wants aren't the same — a need is essential, while a want is more of a preference.

options.label: Only wants matter in a negotiation
options.outcome: Needs actually matter more in a negotiation — telling them apart from wants helps you focus on what's essential.

slides.title: Notice clues, then ask
slides.text: Tone, hesitation, or silence can suggest there is more to the story—but do not guess what someone is thinking. Ask respectfully: "You seem unsure. Is there something about the plan that worries you?"

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone seems hesitant about a plan. What's the respectful next step?

options.label: Ask them directly instead of guessing
options.outcome: Exactly right! Tone, hesitation, or silence can suggest there's more to the story, but asking respectfully is better than guessing.

options.label: Assume you know what they are thinking
options.outcome: Assuming you know what they're thinking can lead to misunderstanding — asking respectfully is a better approach.

options.label: Ignore the hesitation completely
options.outcome: Ignoring hesitation can miss something important — asking about it respectfully is a better next step.

slides.title: Explain your own why
slides.text: Negotiation works better when both sides understand each other. Explain not only what you want, but why it matters to you.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're negotiating something important. Does explaining why it matters to you help?

options.label: Yes — negotiation works better when both sides understand each other
options.outcome: Exactly right! Negotiation works better when both sides understand each other — explaining why something matters helps a lot.

options.label: No, only what you want matters, never why
options.outcome: Why something matters to you actually helps a lot — it's not just about what you want, but the reason behind it.

options.label: Explaining your reasons never changes anything
options.outcome: Explaining your reasons can actually change a lot — it helps the other side understand and consider your request.

slides.title: Find the shared interest
slides.text: People can disagree on the solution while caring about the same thing. Two siblings fighting over movie choice may both really want their opinion to count, so taking turns choosing can solve the deeper issue.

widgetConfig.scenario: Two siblings fight over movie choice. What's often the deeper shared interest?

options.label: Both want their opinion to count, so taking turns choosing can help
options.outcome: Exactly right! People can disagree on the solution while caring about the same deeper thing — here, both wanting their opinion to count.

options.label: There is never a shared interest in a disagreement
options.outcome: There's often a shared interest hiding underneath a disagreement — finding it can solve the deeper issue.

options.label: Only the specific movie matters, nothing deeper
options.outcome: The specific movie often isn't the deepest issue — finding the shared interest underneath, like wanting a say, helps more.

quiz.question: A friend's position is "I want to pick the movie every time," but their interest is "I never get a say." What does this reveal?
choices: A position is what someone says they want; an interest is why
They mean exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: A position is the specific thing someone asks for, while an interest is the deeper reason behind it. A friend's position of "I always pick the movie" might really come from wanting their opinion to matter, which opens up other solutions.

quiz.question: Before asking for a later curfew, why think through your reason and anticipate concerns first?
choices: It makes you more persuasive and ready for pushback
Preparing wastes time
quiz.explanation: Preparing beforehand makes your case far stronger than asking on the spot. Thinking through your reason, guessing what concern they'll raise, and having an answer ready shows you've genuinely thought it through.

quiz.question: You say "so you're saying you're worried about how I'll get home." What does repeating back what you heard show?
choices: That you understand the other person
That you agree with everything they said
quiz.explanation: Repeating back what you heard shows you understand someone, without meaning you automatically agree with them. It can also reveal their real concern is safety, not the clock.

quiz.question: You ask for a later curfew but what you really want is just one late night for a concert. Why does getting clear on this matter?
choices: It leads to a request that's easier to say yes to
It has no effect on the conversation
quiz.explanation: Getting clear on what you actually want makes your request easier to agree to. Asking for one specific late night for a concert is a much smaller ask than requesting a permanent later curfew.

quiz.question: Which question is more likely to reveal what someone really cares about?
choices: "What matters most to you about this?"
"Can I do this, yes or no?"
quiz.explanation: An open-ended question invites a real answer instead of a flat yes or no. Asking what matters most about splitting a chore uncovers what someone actually cares about.

quiz.question: What's the difference between a want and a need in a negotiation?
choices: A need is essential; a want is something you'd simply prefer
They always mean exactly the same thing
quiz.explanation: A need is something that has to happen, while a want is just something you'd prefer. Knowing a working laptop is a need but the newest model is only a want helps you negotiate a device budget more honestly.

quiz.question: A friend goes quiet whenever a certain topic comes up, but says nothing is wrong. What might that suggest?
choices: There might be something worth asking about respectfully
You already know exactly what they are thinking
quiz.explanation: Silence or hesitation can be a clue, but it is not proof. Ask respectfully instead of guessing what your friend thinks.

quiz.question: Why explain your own reason, not just ask what the other person wants?
choices: It helps them understand your side too
Your reasons are never relevant to them
quiz.explanation: Sharing your own reason, not just asking what the other person wants, helps them understand your side too. Explaining why the curfew matters makes the request feel less random.

quiz.question: Two siblings both want to feel like their movie pick matters. What do they actually share?
choices: The same underlying interest, even with different picks
Nothing at all in common
quiz.explanation: Two people can want different things on the surface while sharing the very same underlying interest. Both siblings really just want their opinion to matter, which a rotating pick schedule can solve for both.

quiz.question: Your friend explains a worry, and you summarize it back to check you understood. What is this called?
choices: Active listening
Ignoring them
quiz.explanation: Active listening means checking that you understood correctly, not just letting words go in one ear and out the other. Summarizing a friend's worry back shows you were really paying attention.

slides.title: Create several options
slides.text: Do not get stuck on the first idea. Listing several possible solutions gives you more chances to find one that works for both sides.

widgetConfig.scenario: You and a sibling disagree on which movie to watch, and you only came up with two choices, both rejected. What's a smarter next step?

options.label: Brainstorm a few more options instead of just the first two
options.outcome: Great thinking! Generating more options often reveals a choice that works for everyone, instead of getting stuck between just two.

options.label: Keep arguing about the same two choices
options.outcome: Getting stuck on the same two options that are both rejected rarely leads anywhere — creating new options helps.

options.label: Give up on watching a movie together
options.outcome: Before giving up, brainstorming a few more options might reveal something you both actually like.

slides.title: Make fair trade-offs
slides.text: A trade-off means giving something that matters less to you in exchange for something that matters more. For example, you might agree to send a check-in text in exchange for a later curfew.

widgetConfig.scenario: You want something and are willing to give up something else in exchange that matters less to you. What is this called?

options.label: A trade-off
options.outcome: Exactly right! A trade-off means giving something that matters less to you in exchange for something you want more.

options.label: A punishment
options.outcome: It's not a punishment — giving up something less important for something you want more is called a trade-off.

options.label: There is no way to exchange things in a negotiation
options.outcome: There is a way — making fair trade-offs is a core part of how negotiations work.

slides.title: Compromise is not losing
slides.text: A good compromise protects something important for both sides. Neither person gets every detail they wanted, but both get enough to accept the plan.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your group wants to do a group project your way, but a teammate suggests a mix of both your ideas. How should you respond?

options.label: Consider it seriously — a blended idea might be stronger
options.outcome: Exactly — compromise often produces a better result than either original idea alone. It's not losing, it's combining strengths.

options.label: Insist on doing it exactly your way
options.outcome: Insisting on only your way can mean missing out on a stronger combined idea — and it can frustrate your teammates.

options.label: Give in completely even though you liked your idea
options.outcome: You don't have to abandon your idea completely — a real compromise usually keeps the best parts of both.

slides.title: Protect the relationship
slides.text: When you negotiate with friends or family, how you treat the person matters after the deal is over. Winning one argument is not worth damaging trust.

widgetConfig.scenario: You win an argument with a friend but damage their trust in the process. Was it worth it?

options.label: No — winning one argument isn't worth damaging trust
options.outcome: Exactly right! When you negotiate with friends or family, how you treat the person matters — winning isn't worth damaging trust.

options.label: Yes, winning always matters more than the relationship
options.outcome: Winning isn't always worth it — damaging trust with a friend or family member can cost more than the argument was worth.

options.label: How you treat someone after a deal never matters
options.outcome: How you treat someone after a deal actually matters a lot — it's part of protecting the relationship.

slides.title: Trade across different issues
slides.text: You do not have to bargain over only one thing. You might discuss allowance, chores, timing, and responsibilities together to create more possible deals.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're negotiating about chores with a sibling. Do you have to bargain over only one thing?

options.label: No — you can discuss allowance, timing, and responsibilities together
options.outcome: Exactly right! You don't have to bargain over only one thing — discussing several issues together can create more possible deals.

options.label: Yes, only one issue can ever be discussed at a time
options.outcome: You're not limited to one issue at a time — discussing several together can open up more possible deals.

options.label: Combining issues never creates better deals
options.outcome: Combining issues can actually create better deals — it gives both sides more ways to find something that works.

slides.title: Make a specific first ask
slides.text: A clear request is easier to discuss than a vague one. "Could I earn $5 more each week if I also take out the trash?" gives the other person something concrete to respond to.

widgetConfig.scenario: Which request is easier for someone to respond to?

options.label: "Could I earn $5 more each week if I also take out the trash?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A clear, specific request is easier to discuss than a vague one, since it gives something concrete to respond to.

options.label: A vague request with no specifics
options.outcome: A vague request is harder to respond to — a specific one gives the other person something concrete to react to.

options.label: Specific requests are never easier to discuss
options.outcome: Specific requests are actually much easier to discuss — they give the other person something concrete to respond to.

slides.title: Aim for a deal that lasts
slides.text: A deal is stronger when both sides can live with it afterward. Getting slightly less than your ideal may be better than getting everything while the other person feels forced or resentful.

widgetConfig.scenario: You could get everything you want, but the other person would feel forced. Is this a good deal?

options.label: No — a deal both sides can live with tends to last longer
options.outcome: Exactly right! A deal is stronger when both sides can live with it — getting everything while the other feels forced rarely lasts.

options.label: Yes, getting everything is always the best outcome
options.outcome: Getting everything isn't always best if the other person feels forced — a deal both sides accept tends to last longer.

options.label: Whether a deal lasts never matters
options.outcome: Whether a deal lasts actually matters a lot — a deal both sides can live with holds up much better over time.

slides.title: Fair does not always mean 50/50
slides.text: Fairness can balance over time. You might use the shared console longer today for a special event and give your sibling extra time tomorrow.

widgetConfig.scenario: You use the shared console longer today for a special event. Is this automatically unfair?

options.label: Not necessarily — fairness can balance out over time
options.outcome: Exactly right! Fairness can balance over time — using it longer today and giving extra time tomorrow can still be fair.

options.label: Yes, every single day must be split exactly evenly
options.outcome: Fairness doesn't require splitting every single day exactly evenly — it can balance out over time instead.

options.label: Fairness never allows any flexibility
options.outcome: Fairness actually allows flexibility — balancing things out over time can still be completely fair.

slides.title: Swap tasks when it helps
slides.text: Two people can trade chores if both prefer the swap. If you do dishes and your sibling walks the dog, the deal works only if both willingly agree.

widgetConfig.scenario: You do dishes, your sibling walks the dog. When does this trade work?

options.label: Only if both people willingly agree to the swap
options.outcome: Exactly right! Two people can trade chores, but the deal only works if both willingly agree to it.

options.label: Whenever one person decides, regardless of the other
options.outcome: A trade decided by only one person isn't really a fair swap — both people need to willingly agree.

options.label: Swapping chores never actually helps
options.outcome: Swapping chores can actually help a lot, as long as both people willingly agree to the trade.

quiz.question: Instead of only suggesting one idea for splitting chores, you also suggest two backups. Why generate multiple options instead of one?
choices: The first idea is rarely the best one available
One option is always enough
quiz.explanation: Generating several options gives you more ways to solve the problem. The first idea might be good, but comparing alternatives can reveal a better one.

quiz.question: Asking for a later curfew while offering to text a check-in halfway through — what does this make the deal feel like?
choices: A fair trade-off, not just a one-sided ask
Getting everything you asked for
quiz.explanation: Offering something in return, not just asking for something, makes a deal feel balanced instead of one-sided. It shows you're willing to give as well as take.

quiz.question: When you compromise with a friend over which game to play, what actually happens?
choices: You trade a little of what you want to keep things working well
One person always gets everything they want
quiz.explanation: Compromising means trading a little of what you want to keep the relationship working well, not giving up entirely. Splitting time evenly means neither of you gets everything, but neither is ignored either.

quiz.question: Winning an argument with a sibling by being harsh gets you the TV tonight. What might it cost you?
choices: Goodwill you'll want from them later
Nothing, relationships don't factor into negotiation
quiz.explanation: Winning by being harsh can get you what you want tonight, but it costs you goodwill you'll want from that person again later. Relationships you see every day are worth protecting, not just winning against.

quiz.question: Instead of only negotiating your allowance amount, you also offer to take on an extra chore. What does trading across different things do?
choices: Gives you more ways to reach a deal that works for both sides
Makes the negotiation impossible
quiz.explanation: Trading across different issues at once gives both sides more room to find a deal than arguing over one single number. Offering an extra chore for a bit more allowance opens up options that haggling over one dollar amount never would.

quiz.question: Which is a stronger way to start a negotiation?
choices: "Could I get an extra $5 a week for taking out the trash too?"
"Can I just get more money?"
quiz.explanation: A specific, well-thought-out ask is more persuasive than a vague one, because it shows you've actually thought it through. It gives someone something concrete to say yes to.

quiz.question: Why might getting most of what you want with a happy other side beat getting everything with a resentful one?
choices: A resentful deal often causes problems later
Getting everything is always better no matter what
quiz.explanation: A deal that both sides can live with usually lasts better than one that leaves someone feeling pressured or resentful.

quiz.question: You and a friend share a video game, but you want extra time today for a new update. What's a fair approach?
choices: Ask for extra time today and offer extra time back later
Just take the console without asking
quiz.explanation: An uneven split today, balanced by an uneven split back the other way later, can still be fair overall. Getting extra time today, then giving your friend extra time tomorrow, evens things out.

quiz.question: You want your sibling to walk the dog for you tonight. What's a fair way to ask?
choices: Offer to trade one of their chores in return
Just expect them to do it for free
quiz.explanation: Offering something in return can make a request more balanced, but the other person is still free to say no.

quiz.question: A compromise over which game to play with a friend usually means what?
choices: Neither person gets everything, but neither is ignored
One person always gets their full way
quiz.explanation: A good compromise leaves both people with something, even if neither one gets everything they originally wanted. That's different from one person winning completely.

slides.title: Notice strong emotions
slides.text: Excitement, anger, fear, or frustration can change your decisions. If you feel a strong rush, slow down before accepting or rejecting a deal.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're negotiating and start feeling really frustrated and want to just agree to anything to end it. What should you do?

options.label: Notice the frustration and consider pausing before deciding
options.outcome: Good awareness! Strong emotions can lead to decisions you regret — noticing them and pausing helps you think more clearly.

options.label: Agree to anything right away to end the frustration
options.outcome: Deciding while very frustrated often leads to regret — pausing to calm down usually leads to a better decision.

options.label: Ignore your feelings completely and keep going
options.outcome: Ignoring strong emotions can cloud your judgment — noticing them and pausing helps you negotiate more clearly.

slides.title: Know your limit
slides.text: Before a negotiation, decide what you must have and what you will not accept. Your limit should be based on what actually matters, not on trying to "win."

widgetConfig.scenario: You're trading collectible cards and getting excited about a deal, but it would mean giving up more than you're really comfortable with. What should you do?

options.label: Stick to the limit you set before getting caught up in the excitement
options.outcome: Smart move — knowing your limit beforehand helps you avoid giving up too much in the excitement of a negotiation.

options.label: Go past your limit since you're excited
options.outcome: Getting caught up in excitement is exactly when people give up more than they meant to — sticking to your limit protects you.

options.label: Walk away from all trades forever
options.outcome: You don't need to avoid trading altogether — just stick to the limits you set for yourself before you start.

slides.title: Stay curious after a no
slides.text: A no may contain useful information. Ask, "What would need to change for you to consider this later?" and listen to the answer.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone says no to your idea. What might help uncover useful information?

options.label: Ask "What would need to change for you to consider this later?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! A no may contain useful information — asking what would need to change and listening can uncover it.

options.label: Assume the no is final and stop asking anything
options.outcome: Assuming a no is completely final skips a chance to learn what might change it — staying curious can reveal more.

options.label: A no never contains useful information
options.outcome: A no can actually contain useful information — asking a thoughtful follow-up question can reveal it.

slides.title: Respect matters more than winning
slides.text: With friends and family, you will keep interacting after the negotiation ends. Be firm about the issue without insulting, embarrassing, or pressuring the person.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're negotiating with a family member you'll keep seeing afterward. What matters?

options.label: Being firm about the issue without insulting or pressuring them
options.outcome: Exactly right! With friends and family, you'll keep interacting afterward, so being firm without insulting or pressuring them matters.

options.label: Winning at any cost, even if it embarrasses them
options.outcome: Winning at any cost can damage an ongoing relationship — being firm without insulting or embarrassing them works better.

options.label: Respect never matters once a negotiation starts
options.outcome: Respect actually matters a lot, especially with people you'll keep interacting with after the negotiation ends.

slides.title: Recognize pressure tactics
slides.text: Statements like "decide right now" or "everyone else already agreed" can push you to act before thinking. Pressure is a reason to slow down, not speed up.

widgetConfig.prompt: Sort each tactic into Fair or Pressure tactic

items.label: Using guilt to make you feel bad for saying no
Offering to put the agreement in writing
Repeating the same demand louder each time
Asking what would make the deal work for you

slides.title: Ask for thinking time
slides.text: You do not have to answer every offer immediately. "Can I think about it and tell you tomorrow?" is a reasonable response.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone makes you an offer and wants an answer immediately. What's a reasonable thing to say?

options.label: Can I think about it and get back to you tomorrow?
options.outcome: Exactly! Asking for thinking time is a completely reasonable request and helps you avoid a rushed decision.

options.label: You must always answer on the spot
options.outcome: You don't have to answer immediately — asking for time to think it over is a reasonable and smart move.

options.label: Agree right away to avoid seeming difficult
options.outcome: Agreeing right away just to avoid seeming difficult can lead to a decision you regret — asking for time is better.

slides.title: Know when a win costs too much
slides.text: If getting your way would damage trust, embarrass someone, or leave them feeling forced, reconsider whether the deal is worth it.

widgetConfig.scenario: Getting your way would damage trust and leave someone feeling forced. What should you consider?

options.label: Whether the deal is actually worth it
options.outcome: Exactly right! If getting your way would damage trust or leave someone feeling forced, it's worth reconsidering whether the deal is worth it.

options.label: Push for the win regardless of the cost
options.outcome: Pushing for a win regardless of the cost can damage trust in ways that outweigh the benefit — it's worth reconsidering.

options.label: The cost of a win never matters
options.outcome: The cost of a win actually matters a lot — damaged trust can cost more than the win itself was worth.

slides.title: Ask what is behind the no
slides.text: Instead of arguing with a refusal, ask about the concern. "Can you help me understand what worries you about this?" may uncover a problem you can solve.

widgetConfig.scenario: Someone refuses your request. What's more useful than arguing with the refusal?

options.label: Ask about their concern, like "What worries you about this?"
options.outcome: Exactly right! Instead of arguing with a refusal, asking about the concern behind it may uncover a problem you can actually solve.

options.label: Argue harder against the refusal
options.outcome: Arguing harder against a refusal rarely helps — understanding the concern behind it is much more useful.

options.label: There's never a reason behind a refusal worth exploring
options.outcome: There's often a real concern behind a refusal — asking about it can reveal a problem you can actually solve.

slides.title: Renegotiate when things change
slides.text: An agreement can be revisited when circumstances change. If a chore plan no longer works because your schedule changed, bring it up and make a new plan together.

widgetConfig.scenario: A chore plan no longer works because your schedule changed. What should you do?

options.label: Bring it up and make a new plan together
options.outcome: Exactly right! An agreement can be revisited when circumstances change — bringing it up and making a new plan together works well.

options.label: Keep following the old plan even though it does not work
options.outcome: Sticking to a plan that no longer fits your schedule rarely works well — bringing it up for a new plan is better.

options.label: Agreements can never be revisited once made
options.outcome: Agreements actually can be revisited when circumstances change — bringing it up and making a new plan works well.

quiz.question: Why decide your minimum acceptable outcome before a negotiation starts?
choices: It helps you avoid crossing an important limit under pressure
It guarantees you will get exactly what you want
quiz.explanation: Knowing your real limit before emotions rise helps you judge offers clearly. The limit should reflect what you actually need, not a random number chosen just to win.

quiz.question: A guardian says no to a bigger allowance. What is a good next step?
choices: Calmly ask what would need to change for a yes later
Give up on the topic completely
quiz.explanation: A "no" is often the start of a longer conversation, not the end of one. Calmly asking what would need to change for a future yes keeps the door open instead of shutting the topic down.

quiz.question: A trade a friend offers is clearly unfair to you. What is a reasonable response?
choices: Say you'd rather keep what you have
Accept it so you don't seem difficult
quiz.explanation: Walking away from an unfair deal is a reasonable, healthy choice, not something to feel guilty about. You don't have to trade just because someone offered.

quiz.question: You're so excited about a trade you'd agree to almost anything. What should you do?
choices: Notice the excitement and slow down before agreeing
Agree immediately since excitement means it's a good deal
quiz.explanation: Strong feelings like excitement can push you toward agreeing to a deal you'll later regret. Noticing that rush and slowing down gives you a chance to think clearly before saying yes.

quiz.question: Winning an argument with a sibling by being harsh gets you the TV tonight. What might it cost you?
choices: Goodwill you'll want from them later
Nothing at all, relationships aren't affected
quiz.explanation: Being harsh can win you the TV tonight but cost you trust you'll want from your sibling again soon. People you live with remember how you treated them, not just who won.

quiz.question: Someone rushes you to decide right now before you can think. What does that suggest?
choices: It's worth slowing down, not deciding under pressure
You should always decide fast when rushed
quiz.explanation: Being rushed is a reason to slow down and think. Some deadlines are real, so check the facts instead of assuming every deadline is fake.

quiz.question: You're unsure about a deal someone just offered. What can you say?
choices: "Can I think about it and get back to you?"
You must decide on the spot every time
quiz.explanation: Asking for time to think it over is a completely reasonable, complete response on its own. It often leads to a much better decision than answering under pressure.

quiz.question: You could win an argument with your sibling by being harsh. Why might that not be worth it?
choices: It can damage a relationship you'll need again later
Relationships never matter in a negotiation
quiz.explanation: A short-term win can cost you something bigger later, like the trust you'll need the next time you ask your sibling for something. Winning isn't worth it if it damages a relationship you rely on daily.

quiz.question: A guardian says no to your request. What's a good follow-up?
choices: Calmly ask what's behind the no
Assume the answer will never change
quiz.explanation: Understanding the actual reason behind a no can turn a flat refusal into a real conversation. Asking what they're worried about often uncovers a concern you can actually address.

quiz.question: A chore-split deal you made with your sibling stopped working after your schedule changed. What can you do?
choices: Bring it up and renegotiate
Just live with something that no longer works
quiz.explanation: It's fair to revisit a deal once circumstances genuinely change, since an old agreement isn't meant to last forever no matter what. Bringing up a chore split again after a schedule change is reasonable, not unfair.

slides.title: Positions vs. interests
slides.text: A position is the outcome someone asks for; an interest is the reason they care about it. Negotiations improve when you move from "What do you want?" to "Why does that matter?" because several different solutions may satisfy the same interest.

widgetConfig.scenario: Your friend says they want the whole weekend off from a group project (their position), but really they're just worried about having enough time to study for finals (their interest). Which matters more to understand?

options.label: Their interest — the real reason behind the request
options.outcome: Exactly right! A position is what someone says they want, while an interest is the real reason underneath it — understanding the interest often reveals a better solution.

options.label: Only their stated position, nothing else
options.outcome: Focusing only on the stated position can miss the real reason behind it — understanding the interest helps you find a better solution.

options.label: Neither matters in a negotiation
options.outcome: Both can matter, but understanding the real interest behind a position usually leads to a much better outcome.

slides.title: Your BATNA
slides.text: BATNA means Best Alternative to a Negotiated Agreement: your best realistic option if no deal is reached. A strong BATNA keeps you from accepting a poor deal simply because you feel you have no choice.

widgetConfig.scenario: You're negotiating a price for a used item, and the seller won't budge. You know you could get a similar item elsewhere for less. What should you do?

options.label: Mention your alternative calmly, or be ready to walk away
options.outcome: That's exactly what a strong BATNA (best alternative to a negotiated agreement) gives you — real leverage, because you're not desperate for this one deal.

options.label: Agree to the price anyway so the negotiation ends
options.outcome: Without knowing (or using) your alternative, you lose leverage — you end up with a worse deal than you could have gotten.

options.label: Hide the fact you have other options
options.outcome: Your alternative is most useful when it gives you confidence to hold your ground — you don't need to hide it, just know it's there.

slides.title: Anchoring
slides.text: The first serious number or proposal can influence the range of later discussion. That is why an opening offer should be based on evidence—not an extreme number chosen only to manipulate the conversation.

widgetConfig.scenario: In a price negotiation, the first number mentioned tends to strongly influence the final agreed price. What does this illustrate?

options.label: Anchoring — the first number sets a reference point that influences everything after
options.outcome: Exactly — this is anchoring. The first offer sets a psychological reference point that tends to pull the final outcome toward it, which is why opening offers matter.

options.label: The first number mentioned never matters
options.outcome: The first number actually matters a lot — it sets an anchor that influences the rest of the negotiation, even unconsciously.

options.label: Only the final offer matters, not the opening one
options.outcome: The opening offer plays a bigger role than people often realize — it anchors the whole negotiation toward that reference point.

slides.title: Define the real objective
